config.title: Build CSRF protection flow for web clients

intro.title: Build CSRF protection flow for web clients
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) protection flow for web clients using Node.js and JavaScript. You will learn how to generate and validate secure tokens to prevent unauthorized requests from malicious sites. The core programming concepts involve using cryptographic functions to create tokens, storing them in sessions, and verifying them on form submissions. You'll work with Node.js modules like `crypto` for token generation and `express-session` for managing user sessions. By the end, you'll have a functional middleware that secures your web application against CSRF attacks.
intro.usecase: CSRF protection is essential for any web application that processes user-submitted data through forms or API calls. You'll implement this security pattern in banking applications where fund transfers require token validation, e-commerce checkout flows that protect payment submissions, and admin dashboards that secure content management actions. As a Node.js developer, you'll add CSRF tokens to forms in user profile editors, password change interfaces, and settings panels to prevent unauthorized state-changing requests from malicious sites.

objectives: Initialize a CSRF token generation endpoint in a Node.js server
Configure middleware to validate CSRF tokens on protected routes
Integrate CSRF token injection into HTML form responses
Construct client-side JavaScript to extract and attach CSRF tokens to AJAX requests
Apply CSRF protection to both form submissions and API endpoints
Manipulate server responses to include CSRF tokens in appropriate headers
Implement error handling for invalid or missing CSRF tokens

steps.title: Import required Node.js modules
steps.instruction: Import the crypto and express modules using require() statements at the top of your file.
steps.hint: Use require('moduleName') to import Node.js modules. You'll need both crypto for generating tokens and express for creating the web server.
steps.seedCode: // Import crypto and express modules here
steps.expectedOutcome: Your file will have the crypto and express modules available for use in the CSRF protection implementation.
successCriteria: The crypto and express modules are imported using require() statements.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported one module, but you need both crypto and express. Add the missing import.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. Use require() to import both crypto and express modules.

steps.title: Initialize the Express application
steps.instruction: Create an Express app instance by calling the express() function and assign it to a constant named 'app'.
steps.hint: Use the imported express module to create the application instance.
steps.analogousExample:
// Creating an Express app instance
const app = express();

successCriteria: An Express app instance is created and assigned to a constant named 'app'.

steps.title: Configure middleware for parsing request bodies
steps.instruction: Add express.json() and express.urlencoded() middleware to your Express app instance using app.use().
steps.hint: Call app.use() twice: once with express.json() and once with express.urlencoded({ extended: true }).
steps.expectedOutcome: Your Express app will be able to parse JSON and URL-encoded data from incoming client requests.
successCriteria: The app uses both express.json() and express.urlencoded({ extended: true }) middleware.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some middleware, but make sure to include both express.json() and express.urlencoded({ extended: true }).
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've added both middleware functions using app.use().

steps.title: Create a CSRF token generation function
steps.instruction: Create a function named generateCsrfToken that generates and returns a random CSRF token using crypto.randomBytes.
steps.hint: Use crypto.randomBytes to create random bytes, then convert them to a hexadecimal string.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named generateCsrfToken that returns a random hexadecimal string when called.
successCriteria: The generateCsrfToken function exists, uses crypto.randomBytes, and returns a hexadecimal string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function uses crypto.randomBytes and returns the hexadecimal string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't generate a CSRF token correctly. Review how to use crypto.randomBytes and convert to hex.

steps.title: Set up session storage for CSRF tokens
steps.instruction: Create an in-memory object to store CSRF tokens associated with sessions. Name it 'csrfTokens' and initialize it as an empty object.
steps.hint: You can create a simple JavaScript object using const csrfTokens = {};. This will serve as temporary server-side storage.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: creating an in-memory data store
const userSessions = {};
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a server-side storage object ready to associate CSRF tokens with session identifiers.
successCriteria: An object named 'csrfTokens' is declared and initialized as an empty object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created an object named 'csrfTokens' and initialized it as empty ({}).
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a simple JavaScript object to store CSRF tokens. Use 'const csrfTokens = {};'.

steps.title: Create a route to serve the login form with CSRF token
steps.instruction: Define a GET route at '/login' that generates a CSRF token using your generateCsrfToken function, stores it in your session storage object, and returns an HTML form string containing the token in a hidden input field.
steps.hint: Use app.get('/login', ...) to define the route. Inside the route handler, call generateCsrfToken(), store it in your session object, then return a string of HTML with a form that includes a hidden input field for the token.
steps.expectedOutcome: A GET route at '/login' is defined that generates a CSRF token, stores it, and returns an HTML form with the token embedded as a hidden field.
successCriteria: The route is defined with app.get('/login', ...), calls generateCsrfToken(), stores the token in the session object, and returns an HTML form string containing a hidden input field with the token value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the route, but make sure to: 1) Generate a token using generateCsrfToken(), 2) Store it in your session object, and 3) Return an HTML form string with a hidden input field containing the token value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route definition is missing or incomplete. Remember to create a GET route at '/login' that generates a CSRF token, stores it, and returns an HTML form with the token in a hidden field.

steps.title: Create middleware to validate CSRF tokens
steps.instruction: Define a middleware function named 'validateCsrfToken' that checks if incoming POST requests contain a valid CSRF token in the request body.
steps.hint: Create a function that takes three parameters (req, res, next). Inside, check if the request method is POST, then compare the token from req.body with the stored token from the session.
steps.expectedOutcome: A middleware function that validates CSRF tokens for POST requests will be created.
successCriteria: The 'validateCsrfToken' middleware function is defined with proper request validation logic.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a middleware function, but make sure it properly checks for POST requests and validates the token from req.body.
steps.feedbackWrong: The middleware function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function named 'validateCsrfToken' that validates CSRF tokens for POST requests.

steps.title: Apply CSRF validation middleware to protected routes
steps.instruction: Apply the CSRF validation middleware you created earlier to the login submission route that will be created in the next step.
steps.hint: Use app.use() or app.post() with the middleware function name as an argument before the route handler.
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSRF validation middleware is properly configured to protect the login submission route.
successCriteria: CSRF validation middleware is applied to the login submission route using appropriate Express routing methods.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the middleware is applied correctly to the login submission route.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSRF validation middleware needs to be applied to protect the login submission route. Review how to apply middleware in Express routes.

steps.title: Create the login submission route
steps.instruction: Define a POST route for '/login' that processes form data after CSRF validation.
steps.hint: Use app.post() with the path '/login' and a callback function that handles the request and response.
steps.expectedOutcome: A POST route for '/login' is defined to handle login form submissions.
successCriteria: The code includes app.post('/login', callback) with a callback function that accesses req.body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined a POST route for '/login' with a callback function that can process the request.
steps.feedbackWrong: The login submission route is not correctly defined. Ensure you use app.post() with '/login' and include a callback function.

steps.title: Start the Express server
steps.instruction: Add the app.listen() call to start the Express server on port 3000.
steps.hint: Use app.listen() with port number 3000 and a callback function that logs a message when the server starts.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will be ready to accept HTTP requests on port 3000 when you run the application.
successCriteria: app.listen() is called with port 3000 and a callback function that logs a startup message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added app.listen(), but make sure to include both the port number (3000) and a callback function that logs a message when the server starts.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server isn't properly started. You need to call app.listen() with port 3000 and a callback function.
